title: Advaita (Shankara): not-two; rope and snake in full; the Vivekachudamani opening (2 of 7)
hook: dusk, a garden path, and a snake coiled right where you're about to step
tomorrow: Advaita (Shankara): not-two; rope and snake in full; the Vivekachudamani opening (3 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: advaita, not two. The pots and the clay, and Shankara's one reality. Your line: not two. Did you see the clay under something's name? Today, the most famous picture in all of Advaita. Day two hundred eighty-two.

It's dusk. You're walking home along a path, not paying much attention, and suddenly you freeze. Right in front of your foot, a snake. Coiled, dark, still. Your heart slams. Your skin goes cold. You step back so fast you nearly fall. You shout for someone to bring a light. They come with a lamp, hold it up, and there on the path is a piece of old rope. You laugh, a little shakily. And the Advaita teachers say: that moment, the laugh, is the whole of liberation in miniature.
screen: `DUSK ON THE PATH.` → `A SNAKE AT YOUR FOOT.` → `A LAMP. A ROPE.`

segments.voice: The rope and the snake shows up again and again in Advaita, from Gaudapada, remembered as the teacher of Shankara's teacher, onward. Let's walk through it slowly, because every detail is doing work. First: the fear was real. Your heart really pounded. Advaita doesn't say your experience is fake. It says it's pointed at the wrong thing. Second: the snake was never there, but it wasn't nothing either. It was the rope, seen wrong. Everything the snake had, its shape, its coil, its place on the path, it borrowed from the rope. Shankara has a technical word for this: adhyasa, superimposition. Laying one thing over another. Third: what fixed it? Not a stick. You didn't kill the snake. You didn't argue with it. You brought a light. Knowledge doesn't remove the snake; it shows there wasn't one. That's why Shankara says freedom comes through knowledge, not through doing more. Fourth: the rope was never harmed. The snake didn't make it poisonous. When the snake disappears, nothing is lost but the fear. Now the teaching. The world of separate things, separate me here and separate you there, is like the snake: Brahman, the one reality, seen in dim light. The anxiety is real. The separation, Advaita says, is borrowed. And what's needed isn't a battle but a lamp. Shankara uses other pictures too: a shell that glints like silver, one moon that a tired eye sees as two. But the rope stuck. Maybe because everyone has jumped at something harmless in the dark.
screen: `THE FEAR WAS REAL.` · `THE SNAKE WAS THE ROPE, MISSEEN.` · `A LAMP, NOT A STICK.` · `THE ROPE WAS NEVER HARMED.` · then, large: `NOT TWO.`

segments.voice: Sit, and remember a time you were sure of something that turned out not to be so. A noise in the night that was the fridge. A message you read as angry that wasn't. Feel how real the fear was. Then feel the moment of the light coming on: the relief, the small laugh. Breathe in, and let the relief be here now. Breathe out, and let one of today's worries sit in that same light, just to see. The bell holds the time.
Advaita, through the rope and the snake: separation is superimposed on one reality, like a snake seen on a rope at dusk. Knowledge is the lamp.
Your line: not two. Today, when something makes you jump, a message, a noise, a look, ask before you swing the stick: is there a lamp I could bring? Day two hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Advaita teachers use the rope-and-snake example, along with others like the shell mistaken for silver, to explain superimposition (adhyasa) and why they say knowledge, rather than action, brings liberation.

match.prompt: the rope and the snake — tap the pairs.

myth: in Advaita's picture, your fear of the snake was fake
the fear was real; it was pointed at the wrong thing.
the lamp works by removing the snake
the lamp shows there was never a snake; nothing is removed but the fear.
the rope-and-snake example is older than Shankara
it appears in Gaudapada's Karika on the Mandukya Upanishad; tradition places Gaudapada two generations before him.

fork.setup: it's dusk, and there's a snake at your foot. by the Advaita story, what actually ends the danger?
fork.reveal: a lamp. in the light the snake was always a rope. knowledge, not force, ends the fear.

original.note: Sanskrit: rajju (rope) + sarpa (snake): the rope-snake, Advaita's classic example of superimposition.

trapdoor: what you thought: Advaita says the world is fake.
what it means: the separateness is borrowed, like a snake seen on a rope; the reality underneath is one.

what a scholar hears: adhyasa is laid out in the preamble to Shankara's Brahma Sutra commentary (with shell-silver and double-moon examples); the rope-snake appears in Gaudapada's Mandukya Karika 2.17–18.

sources.ref: Gaudapada, Mandukya Karika 2.17–18 (the rope imagined as a snake)
Shankara, Brahma Sutra Bhashya, preamble on superimposition (adhyasa)

notes: Gaudapada as 'the teacher of Shankara's teacher' (Gaudapada → Govinda → Shankara) is traditional; reviewer softened it to 'remembered as' in the teach and the myth answer, since Gaudapada's dates are debated. Confirm.
Mandukya Karika 2.17–18 reference and the adhyasa preamble examples (shell/silver, two moons) recalled from memory; confirm.
Other Vedanta schools reject the rope-snake account of the world; that difference is taught on the Dvaita days (288–294).
